title: Week 06 · AI Detective Lab
description: Week 06 student-facing live learning lab with a midterm preview and nine high-value interactive moments focused on evidence, context, consequence, judgment, and transfer to the discussion and assignment.

steps.label: Midterm Preview
steps.title: What should you expect next Thursday?
steps.lead: The midterm asks whether you can use what you have learned about AI—not simply memorize definitions.
steps.studentTask: Look up. We are starting with the exam format and what strong preparation looks like.
steps.roomInstruction: 25 questions · 100 points · 75 minutes · open note + course materials · no generative AI
steps.mediaOverlay: Use what you know. Don't just memorize it.

runbook.say: The midterm is designed to see whether you can use what we have learned about AI, not simply memorize definitions.
runbook.studentDoes: Listen for the format, question types, and what to study.
runbook.askNext: What part of the exam feels least clear right now?
runbook.watchFor: Questions about time, notes, Testing Services, or AI use.
runbook.ifStuck: Remind students that the exam is open note but timed.
runbook.transition: Let's see which question type feels least comfortable.

slide.title: Midterm: Can You Make Good AI Decisions?
slide.subtitle: The exam is designed to measure whether you can use AI literacy concepts in realistic situations—not simply recognize vocabulary.
bullets: No generative AI during the exam
slide.quote: A question may not ask “Define hallucination.” It may ask you to recognize what is wrong with an AI-generated citation and decide what a student should do.
slide.takeaway: Understand the concepts well enough to use them.

steps.label: Midterm Pulse
steps.title: Which question type feels least comfortable right now?
steps.lead: Choose the one you would most want to practice before the exam.
steps.studentTask: Choose the question type you feel least confident about.
steps.roomInstruction: Commit first. We will reveal the room after everyone votes.
steps.mediaOverlay: Where does the room need the most practice?

runbook.say: There are three kinds of questions. Which one makes you want the most practice?
runbook.askNext: Why do you think that category feels harder?
runbook.landHere: The hardest questions are not necessarily the ones with the hardest vocabulary—they require judgment.
runbook.watchFor: A strong cluster around judgment cases.
runbook.ifStuck: Define each category in one sentence.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most of the room has voted and results are discussed.
runbook.transition: Now let's make those three levels concrete.

slide.title: Which Type of Question Feels Hardest?
slide.subtitle: Your answer helps us decide where to spend our review energy today.
columns: “A student receives fake citations. What should they do?”
“Should an organization trust an AI recommendation?”
slide.takeaway: Commit before you see the room.

steps.label: Exam Structure
steps.title: Three levels of thinking
steps.studentTask: Notice how the point values increase as the thinking becomes more applied.
steps.roomInstruction: Foundations = recognize. Application = use. Judgment = decide.

runbook.say: The first 10 questions check foundations. The next 10 ask you to apply concepts. The final 5 are richer judgment cases and are worth the most points.
runbook.studentDoes: Connect each level to a way of studying.
runbook.askNext: What would be a bad way to study for an exam built this way?
runbook.landHere: Memorizing definitions alone will not prepare you for 80 percent of the points.
runbook.watchFor: Students realizing they need scenario practice.
runbook.ifStuck: Contrast memorizing 'bias' with recognizing bias in a case.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain the difference between the three sections.
runbook.transition: Today's lab is practice for exactly that kind of judgment.

slide.title: The Questions Get Harder Because the Decisions Get Bigger
slide.subtitle: The point values increase as the thinking becomes more complex.
columns: Recognize and understand key AI literacy concepts.
Use course concepts in realistic situations.
Evaluate evidence, risk, stakeholders, and consequences.
slide.callout: Same topic, three levels: What is bias? → What concern does this situation show? → What should the organization do?

steps.label: Framework Reboot
steps.title: CLAIM → CHECK → CONTEXT → CONSEQUENCE → CALL
steps.lead: No notes. What does each move mean?
steps.studentTask: Say the five moves out loud with the room.
steps.roomInstruction: What exactly is it saying? What evidence matters? What's missing? What if it's wrong? What should we do?

runbook.say: Let's see what survived from Tuesday.
runbook.studentDoes: Recall the five moves without notes.
runbook.askNext: What are our three possible calls?
runbook.ifStuck: Prompt one word at a time.
runbook.advanceWhen: The room can reconstruct the framework.

slide.title: The AI Detective Framework
slide.subtitle: When an AI answer looks polished or confident, use these five moves.
columns: Separate the output into checkable statements.
Use sources that fit the exact claim.
Look for assumptions, limits, bias, uncertainty, or outdated information.
What happens if it is wrong?
The stakes determine how much verification is appropriate.
slide.quote: AI says: “This is the best laptop for every student.”
slide.takeaway: Your job is not to be impressed. Your job is to make a judgment.

steps.label: Believe the Bot · 1
steps.title: AI says Norse Commons closes at 8:00 tonight.
steps.studentTask: Vote based on what you would actually do.

runbook.say: Don't overthink it. What would you really do?
runbook.askNext: What source would settle this quickly?
runbook.landHere: Low stakes can still deserve a quick authoritative check.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask where official hours would live.
runbook.advanceWhen: The room names an appropriate source.
runbook.transition: Now raise the cost of being wrong.

slide.title: AI Says: Norse Commons Closes at 8 PM
slide.subtitle: A confident answer is still a claim that can be checked.
bullets: What would you check before walking over?
What source would settle this quickly?
How much verification is reasonable for a low-stakes decision?

steps.label: Believe the Bot · 4
steps.title: AI recommends doubling an over-the-counter medication dose because symptoms are severe.
steps.studentTask: Vote based on the consequence of being wrong.

runbook.say: Notice how your verification threshold changes when health is involved.
runbook.askNext: What kind of evidence or human expertise is appropriate here?
runbook.watchFor: Authoritative medical information or qualified professional.
runbook.ifStuck: Compare this with checking restaurant hours.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain why stakes matter.

slide.title: Same Confidence. Very Different Stakes.
slide.subtitle: AI recommends doubling an over-the-counter medication dose because symptoms are severe.
bullets: What could happen if the advice is wrong?
What kind of source or human expertise is appropriate?
slide.takeaway: The consequence of error changes the verification you need.

steps.label: Compare the Stakes
steps.title: Same AI confidence. Different consequences.
steps.lead: Concert date · Course policy · Medication advice
steps.studentTask: Look at the three situations and decide why the amount and type of checking should change.
steps.roomInstruction: A confident answer can still deserve very different verification depending on what happens if it is wrong.

runbook.say: The AI can sound equally confident in all three situations. What changes is what happens if the answer is wrong.
runbook.studentDoes: Compare the verification needed for a concert date, course policy, and medication advice.
runbook.askNext: Where would you tolerate the least uncertainty?
runbook.watchFor: Students naming authoritative sources and human expertise.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask what harm follows from a wrong answer in each case.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain why verification depth changes.
runbook.transition: Now practice breaking a polished answer into checkable claims.

slide.title: Same AI Confidence. Different Consequences.
slide.subtitle: An answer can sound equally polished in every context while deserving very different levels of trust.
columns: Check an official venue or ticket source.
Check the syllabus, Canvas, or instructor.
Use authoritative information or qualified professional guidance.

steps.label: Spot the Claims
steps.title: How many separate claims are hiding here?
steps.lead: “NKU students get free parking after 5 p.m., all first-year students qualify for a technology grant, and the library stays open until midnight every weekday.”
steps.studentTask: Type the separate claims you would investigate. Short phrases are fine.
steps.roomInstruction: FICTIONAL CLASSROOM SCENARIO — do not treat these statements as real NKU information.
steps.mediaOverlay: One sentence can contain multiple claims.

runbook.say: This is a fictional classroom scenario. Your job is to pull it apart.
runbook.askNext: Which claim would be easiest to verify first?
runbook.landHere: You cannot check an answer well until you know exactly what it is claiming.
runbook.watchFor: Students identifying at least three distinct claims.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask them to underline every statement that could be true or false.
runbook.transition: Once you have a claim, the next problem is choosing evidence.

slide.title: One Sentence Can Hide Multiple Claims
slide.subtitle: FICTIONAL CLASSROOM SCENARIO — do not treat these statements as real NKU information.
slide.quote: “NKU students get free parking after 5 PM, all first-year students qualify for technology grants, and the library stays open until midnight.”
bullets: How many separate claims are here?
Which claim would be easiest to verify first?
Which source would be strongest for each?
slide.callout: Respond with the number of separate claims you see.
slide.takeaway: You cannot verify an answer until you know exactly what it is claiming.

steps.label: Source Battle
steps.title: Best source for: Can I park overnight on campus?
steps.lead: Choose the strongest starting source for this exact question.
steps.studentTask: Choose the strongest source for the claim—not the source you would click first.
steps.roomInstruction: Best source for WHAT exact claim?

runbook.say: Source quality is not one permanent ranking. It depends on what you are trying to know.
runbook.askNext: Would your answer change if the question were 'What is parking like after 5 p.m.?'
runbook.landHere: Authority and usefulness depend on the claim.
runbook.watchFor: Students recognizing that experience-based sources can answer different questions.
runbook.transition: Now you will investigate your own AI output.

slide.title: What Source Would You Trust?
slide.subtitle: Scenario: “Can I park overnight on campus?”
columns: May show someone's experience, but not necessarily the current rule.
Useful context, but not authoritative policy.
Best starting point for the current rule.
slide.callout: Vote for the strongest starting source.
slide.takeaway: The best source depends on what you are trying to know.

steps.label: Choose Your Output
steps.title: Pick one AI output worth investigating.
steps.lead: Choose something with at least three claims, details, assumptions, or recommendations you can check.
steps.studentTask: Choose or generate one safe AI output. Good options: study guide, recommendation, explanation, travel idea, career advice, product recommendation, or AI visual.
steps.roomInstruction: If there isn't much to investigate, choose a better output.
steps.mediaOverlay: Choose something you can actually investigate.

runbook.say: The quality of your lab depends on choosing an output with enough substance to check.
runbook.studentDoes: Select one AI output and save it.
runbook.askNext: Can you identify three things in it that could be checked?
runbook.landHere: Three checkable items is the threshold.
runbook.watchFor: Students choosing vague or purely creative outputs.
runbook.ifStuck: Offer study guide, scholarship advice, laptop recommendation, career advice, or Cincinnati weekend plan.

slide.title: Choose an AI Output Worth Investigating
slide.subtitle: Pick something with enough substance to identify at least three claims, details, assumptions, or recommendations.
columns: Study plan · career advice · travel plan · scholarship advice
A joke, poem, or simple decorative image gives you little to verify.
slide.callout: SAVE THE ORIGINAL AI OUTPUT. You will need it for your evidence trail.
slide.takeaway: If there isn't much to investigate, choose a better output.

steps.label: Main Investigation
steps.title: PROVE IT.
steps.lead: Your goal is not to catch AI being wrong. Your goal is to find out what the evidence actually supports.
steps.studentTask: Identify three claims/details/assumptions. Check at least two using appropriate sources. Record what you found and label each Supported, Partially Supported, Unsupported, or Can't Verify.
steps.roomInstruction: Open the source. Read what it actually says. Do not stop at the search result.

runbook.say: Work independently or quietly with a partner nearby. I am going to circulate and ask you about your evidence.
runbook.studentDoes: Investigate at least two claims and document the evidence.
runbook.askNext: Does your source actually support the claim—or just look related to it?
runbook.landHere: Evidence is a relationship between a claim and what a source actually supports.
runbook.watchFor: Google snippets, weak sources, outdated dates, partial support, and inability to verify.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask: What exactly is the claim? Who would be authoritative on it? Is the information current?
runbook.advanceWhen: Students have at least two meaningful checks.

slide.title: PROVE IT.
slide.subtitle: Your goal is not to catch AI being wrong. Your goal is to find out what the evidence actually supports.
numbered: Identify 3 claims, details, assumptions, or recommendations.
Choose the strongest source for each.
Open the source—do not stop at the search result.
Read what the source actually says.
Label each: Supported · Partially Supported · Unsupported · Can't Verify.
slide.callout: TARGET FOR CLASS: Complete at least 2 strong checks and start the third.

steps.label: Plot Twist
steps.title: What changed when you actually checked?
steps.lead: Share one surprise from your investigation.
steps.studentTask: Submit one short finding: outdated, partial, unsupported, conflicting, missing, or can't verify.
steps.roomInstruction: Examples: outdated date · source mismatch · partial support · missing requirement · conflicting sources
steps.placeholder: I thought ___, but when I checked ___, I found...

runbook.say: Give me one plot twist from the room.
runbook.landHere: Can't verify does not mean false. It means you do not have enough evidence yet.
runbook.ifStuck: Invite examples of partial support, not only wrong answers.
runbook.advanceWhen: Two or three room examples have been discussed.
runbook.transition: Facts are only part of evaluation. Now ask what the answer forgot.

slide.title: What Changed When You Actually Checked?
slide.subtitle: Good evaluation can change your first impression—even when the AI was not completely wrong.
columns: Date, policy, price, hours, or availability may have moved.
The source supports a narrower claim than AI made.
Don't turn uncertainty into a false claim of certainty.
slide.callout: Complete: “I thought ___, but after checking ___, I found ___.”

steps.label: Perspective Flip
steps.title: What can be missing even when some facts are correct?
steps.lead: AI says: “Every first-year college student should buy a car because it makes college easier.”
steps.studentTask: Name one missing factor AND one person or group whose perspective could change the recommendation.
steps.roomInstruction: Think: cost · insurance · parking · transit · accessibility · housing · income · ability to drive
steps.mediaOverlay: Correct facts can still produce bad advice.

runbook.say: Technically correct details can still lead to a poor recommendation when context is missing.
runbook.studentDoes: Identify missing context and a stakeholder perspective.
runbook.askNext: How would that person's situation change the recommendation?
runbook.landHere: Context and perspective affect usefulness and fairness.
runbook.watchFor: Students moving beyond generic 'bias' language to specific assumptions.
runbook.ifStuck: Compare commuter vs resident, or higher-income vs limited-income student.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain why a perspective changes the answer.

slide.title: Who Did AI Forget?
slide.subtitle: AI says: “Every student should buy a car because it makes college easier.”
columns: Commuter · resident · parent · student with limited money
slide.callout: Choose TWO perspectives and explain how they might change the recommendation.
slide.takeaway: Correct facts can still produce bad advice when context is missing.

steps.label: Consequence + Call
steps.title: Your AI output: Trust, Revise, or Reject?
steps.lead: Before you vote, ask: What happens if someone relies on this and it is wrong?
steps.studentTask: Consider the consequence first, then vote on your own AI output.
steps.roomInstruction: TRUST · REVISE · REJECT — What evidence would make you switch?

runbook.say: Your final call should reflect both the evidence you found and the consequence of being wrong.
runbook.studentDoes: Consider consequence, then vote Trust, Revise, or Reject.
runbook.askNext: What evidence would make you switch your call?
runbook.landHere: A responsible call is evidence-based and can change when better evidence appears.
runbook.watchFor: Students explaining why their call fits the stakes.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask whether the output is usable as-is, needs changes, or should not be used.
runbook.transition: Everything you just did can now become your discussion and assignment.

slide.title: Trust, Revise, or Reject?
slide.subtitle: Use both the evidence you found and the consequence of being wrong.
columns: There is value, but something important needs correction or context.
Fix it before relying on it.
The output is too unsupported, misleading, or risky.
slide.callout: Vote on YOUR AI output. Then ask: What evidence would make you switch your call?
slide.takeaway: A good decision can change when better evidence appears.

steps.label: Turn It In
steps.title: Today's investigation already did most of the setup work.
steps.lead: Discussion = short + social. Assignment = full evidence trail.
steps.studentTask: Discussion: choose your most interesting claim, add two perspectives, a responsible next step, and a closing question. Assignment: finish at least three documented checks and your full Trust / Revise / Reject reasoning.
steps.roomInstruction: Before you leave, know your next move.

runbook.say: Do not start over. Reuse the evidence you created today.
runbook.studentDoes: Choose what will become the discussion and what still needs work for the 50-point assignment.
runbook.askNext: What is the smallest next step you still owe?
runbook.landHere: The discussion is one focused argument. The assignment is the full evidence trail.
runbook.watchFor: Students assuming they need two completely different examples.
runbook.ifStuck: Tell them they may reuse today's output if it has enough substance.

slide.kicker: TURN TODAY'S WORK INTO YOUR SUBMISSION
slide.title: Do Not Start Over.
slide.subtitle: Today's investigation is the raw material for both Week 06 deliverables.
columns: Choose one interesting claim. Explain your check, context, consequence, call, two perspectives, responsible next step, and a question for classmates.
Document at least three checks, evidence quality, missing context, consequence, decision, safeguard, reflection, and AI-use documentation.
slide.callout: Before you leave: identify the ONE smallest next step you still need to complete.
slide.takeaway: Discussion = explain your judgment. Assignment = prove your evaluation process.

steps.label: Exit Pulse
steps.title: What will now make you suspicious instead of impressed?
steps.lead: Name one feature of AI output that you will treat differently after this week.
steps.roomInstruction: Examples: confident wording · exact statistics · citations · official-sounding names · polished tables · long explanations
steps.placeholder: I will be more suspicious when AI...
steps.mediaOverlay: Don't just tell me whether AI was right. Show me how you know.

runbook.say: Give me one thing AI can do that will now make you pause instead of automatically trust it.
runbook.askNext: What will you do differently when you see it?
runbook.landHere: AI literacy is not suspicion of everything. It is better judgment about what deserves trust.

slide.title: What Will You Never Unsee?
slide.subtitle: What AI behavior will now make you pause and verify instead of automatically trust?
slide.quote: Don't just tell me whether AI was right. Show me how you know.
slide.callout: Submit one sentence: “I will be more suspicious when AI…”
slide.takeaway: AI literacy is not distrusting everything. It is knowing what deserves trust.
